sections.title: A visit to a community recording studio

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The plan shows the recording studio from above. The central junction is marked with a cross, and north is at the top. Walk quietly, as some rooms are in use.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The control room is north of the junction. The top path ends at a wide window where you can see the equipment.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The voice booth is east of the junction, off the right-hand path. Its heavy door is kept closed between sessions.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The equipment store is south of the junction. At the bottom of the plan you will see a small square room.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The listening room is west of the junction. The left-hand passage leads directly to its entrance.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Put phones in silent mode before entering. The recording in the main booth may continue while we look through the window.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: We will use a short piece of speech for the first demonstration. Music will be recorded in the following session.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Clean headphones are in the drawer. The items on top of the bench have already been used.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The red light beside a door shows that the room is in use. Wait until it goes out before entering.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The evening group meets in the lobby. There is no need to go straight to a booth.

sections.title: How an echo gives information about distance

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: When a sound reaches a surface and returns, its delay can tell us something about the path it followed. We will observe the difference between a direct sound and a return.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A clap gives a short starting sound. It is easier to separate from a later return than a long sound.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The first sound reaches the microphone directly. The next sound may have travelled farther before reaching it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The echo has a longer path. It goes from the source to a reflecting surface and then back towards the microphone.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Try a large flat wall for the first comparison. A complex surface may send the sound in several directions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Leave the microphone on the same stand while you move the source. This keeps one position fixed.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Make a small mark on the floor for the source. You can then return to the same position later.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Look at the recorded waveform. It can show a gap that is hard to measure simply by listening.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: If nearby noise hides the return, repeat the recording when the room is quieter.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A long sound can continue while its echo arrives. That overlap makes the delay harder to see.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Record the distance from the source to the wall. You will need it when comparing two arrangements.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The timing gives one clue about the route of the sound. Report where the source and microphone were placed before drawing a conclusion about distance.
